newsitem.title: UK: Several held after N.Irish police murder.
newsitem.headline: Several held after N.Irish police murder.

text.p: Northern Ireland police arrested several people on Sunday after an off-duty police officer was beaten to death outside a bar, apparently by a Protestant mob.

Father of three Gregory Taylor, 45, was killed in the town of Ballymoney in County Antrim. Television reports said at least seven pro-British "Loyalists", angered by a recent ban on a Protestant march, set on him in the street in the early hours of Sunday morning.
"A number of arrests have been made. Inquiries are ongoing," a Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) spokesman said, adding that Taylor "died from injuries received when he was violently assaulted".

Protestant hardliners have been infuriated in recent months at being prevented from holding marches in the County Antrim village of Dunloy because of objections by its mainly Roman Catholic Irish nationalist residents.

Britain's Northern Ireland secretary, Mo Mowlam, who was appointed to the sensistive Northern Ireland post a month ago after the Labour Party ended 18 years of Conservative rule with a landslide general election victory, condemned the killing.
"Any death in circumstances like these must be utterly condemned and our thoughts at this minute are with the immediate family of the deceased," she said in a statement.
In west Belfast security forces found a bomb detonation wire as they investigated an IRA claim that it had abandoned a defused landmine in the predominantly Catholic district, police said,

An Irish Republican Army statement hinted that one of its units had aborted a planned attack on security forces on Saturday and left the landmine in a van in the Poleglass district, a staunch Irish nationalist area.
It was the IRA's first reported hostile action in the province for six weeks, during which Britain has resumed contacts broken off 16 months ago with their political wing.
Protestant politicians immediately called for the tentative contacts to be abandoned.
The vehicle was set on fire overnight following the IRA's claim made in a coded telephone call to a local radio station.
Children told journalists they had played inside the suspiciously parked vehicle before the fire and that it contained two containers of white powder.
Police said a security operation was continuing but there was no early sign that they had found any other bomb parts.
"The area has been sealed off. A full clearance operation has begun," the RUC spokesman said. "A command wire has been found and a (precautionary) controlled explosion has been carried out."
The IRA, which has frequently left bombs in nationalist zones to catch passing British patrols, said it dumped the bomb after defusing it because civilians were nearby.
Security sources, unsure whether it was a hoax to lure them into a booby trap, said they were treating the alert as a "real terrorist threat".

Britain ended contacts with the IRA's political arm Sinn Fein in February 1996 when the guerrillas scrapped a 17-month ceasefire by setting off a huge bomb in the Docklands area of London's East End, killing two people.
After winning power on May 1, Prime Minister Tony Blair resumed talks between government officials and Sinn Fein.
But Blair made clear the talks could only take place if the IRA refrained from using violence. Two rounds of talks have been held in the past 10 days and another is due soon.
